AIPE Sample Size Planning for an Equivalence Test on the Standardized Mean Difference

Source: R/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd.R
ss_aipe_equivalence_smd.Rd

Computes the smallest per-group sample size at which the confidence interval that equivalence_smd reports, the 100(1 - 2\(\alpha\))% interval on the standardized mean difference whose position against the equivalence bounds decides the two one-sided tests (Lakens, 2017), is no wider than width when the sample standardized mean difference equals the planning value true_smd (accuracy in parameter estimation, AIPE; Kelley & Rausch, 2006). With the conventional \(\alpha = .05\) the interval is the 90% interval. With assurance the function returns the smallest per-group sample size at which the realized interval is no wider than width with at least that probability.

Usage

ss_aipe_equivalence_smd(
  true_smd = 0,
  width,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  assurance = NULL,
  balanced = TRUE
)

Arguments

true_smd

Planning value of the population standardized mean difference \(\delta\), a single finite number. Default 0. The interval is narrowest when the sample standardized mean difference is 0, so for a given width the plan at 0 is the smallest over planning values.

width

Target full width of the interval on the standardized mean difference scale (e.g., 0.20 for a 90% interval of width 0.20).

alpha_level

One-sided significance level of each of the two tests. The interval planned for is at confidence level \(1 - 2\alpha\), as in equivalence_smd. Default 0.05 (90% interval).

assurance

Optional probability in \((0, 1)\) that the realized interval is no wider than width. The function returns the smallest per-group sample size, at or above the one planned without it, at which that probability is at least assurance (Kelley, Maxwell, & Rausch, 2003; Kelley & Rausch, 2006). Default NULL (the plan is for the width at true_smd only).

balanced

Logical; TRUE (default) plans equal-\(n\) groups. Unequal-\(n\) planning is not yet supported.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value and one row per term:

necessary_n_per_group

the planned sample size of each group.

total_N

twice necessary_n_per_group.

width

the target width, as given.

true_smd

the planning value.

expected_width

the full width of the interval equivalence_smd reports with necessary_n_per_group in each group when the sample standardized mean difference equals true_smd, that is, ci_upper minus ci_lower of equivalence_smd(smd = true_smd, n_1 = n, n_2 = n, alpha_level = alpha_level) with n the planned size. It is no larger than width. Without assurance, the same interval with one fewer case in each group is wider than width, unless the plan is the smallest size, 2 per group.

assurance

the requested probability; present only when assurance was given.

assurance_attained

the probability, with necessary_n_per_group in each group and population standardized mean difference true_smd, that the realized interval is no wider than width; present only when assurance was given. It is computed, not simulated (see Details), and it is at least assurance.

The conf_level attribute records the confidence level of the interval, \(1 - 2\alpha\).

Details

The interval planned for. equivalence_smd reports the interval $$\hat d \pm t_{1 - \alpha,\, n_1 + n_2 - 2} \sqrt{\frac{n_1 + n_2}{n_1 n_2} + \frac{\hat d^{\,2}}{2 (n_1 + n_2)}},$$ a large-sample standard error of \(\hat d\) with a critical value from Student's t distribution on \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom, and it declares equivalence when that interval lies inside the bounds. This function plans for the same interval, because it is the interval the analysis reports; a plan for any other interval would describe a width the analysis does not show. With \(n\) in each group the width is $$w(\hat d, n) \;=\; t_{1 - \alpha,\, 2n - 2} \sqrt{(8 + \hat d^{\,2}) / n}.$$ The plan is the smallest \(n\) of at least 2 with \(w(\delta, n) \le \omega\), where \(\delta\) is true_smd and \(\omega\) is width. Because \(w\) decreases in \(n\), the interval with \(n - 1\) in each group is wider than \(\omega\). The search starts at \(z_{1 - \alpha}^2 (8 + \delta^2) / \omega^2\), the answer with the standard normal quantile in place of the t quantile, which is not above the answer because the t quantile is the larger.

Assurance. Without assurance the plan makes the interval no wider than the target when the sample standardized mean difference equals true_smd; a sample with a larger \(|\hat d|\) gives a wider interval. With assurance the function finds the sample size at which the realized interval is no wider than the target with at least that probability, from the sampling distribution of \(\hat d\), as Kelley and Rausch (2006, pp. 372–373) do for the noncentral t interval:

  1. At a given \(n\) the width depends on the sample only through \(\hat d\) and increases with \(|\hat d|\), so the interval is no wider than \(\omega\) exactly when \(|\hat d| \le c(n)\), where \(c(n)^2 = n \omega^2 / t_{1 - \alpha,\, 2n - 2}^2 - 8\). When \(c(n)^2 \le 0\), even the interval at \(\hat d = 0\) is wider than \(\omega\) and the probability is 0.

  2. For two independent samples from normal populations with a common variance, \(T = \hat d \sqrt{n / 2}\) is the two-group t statistic, distributed as noncentral t on \(\nu = 2n - 2\) degrees of freedom with noncentrality \(\lambda = \delta \sqrt{n / 2}\). The probability is \(P_n = P(|T| \le c(n) \sqrt{n / 2})\), the form of Kelley and Rausch (2006, Equation 20). With \(T = (Z + \lambda) / \sqrt{V / \nu}\), where \(Z\) is standard normal and \(V\) is chi square on \(\nu\) degrees of freedom, independent of \(Z\), $$P(|T| \le k) \;=\; E_V\Big[\Phi\big(k \sqrt{V / \nu} - \lambda\big) - \Phi\big(-k \sqrt{V / \nu} - \lambda\big)\Big],$$ which is computed by numerical integration over \(V\). Only the normal distribution function and the chi square density enter, because R's noncentral t distribution function is an approximation at noncentrality values above 37.62, which plans for narrow intervals reach.

  3. The function returns the smallest \(n\), at or above the sample size planned without assurance, with \(P_n \ge\) assurance, found by doubling a step upward and then bisecting. assurance_attained is \(P_n\) at that \(n\).

The probability is exact for the normal model, up to numerical integration. Nothing is simulated, so the function draws no random numbers and returns the same plan on every call. The probability agreed with R's noncentral t distribution function to within \(10^{-10}\) wherever that function is accurate, and with simulation from normal scores: in 24 planning conditions of 20,000 simulated studies each, the proportion of intervals no wider than the target at the planned size differed from \(P_n\) by at most 2.0 Monte Carlo standard errors.

Three properties of the step are worth knowing.

  • The answer is never below the sample size planned without assurance, and an assurance at or below the probability at that size returns it unchanged. At or above that size \(P_n\) did not decrease in any of 48 planning conditions scanned over every whole \(n\) (6,639 sizes in all).

  • At true_smd = 0 the plan without assurance often meets a moderate request already. The probability at that size depends on how far rounding up to a whole number narrows the interval: over widths from 0.05 to 3 at \(\alpha = .05\) it ranged from .11 to .97, with a median of .85, and for a width of 0.50 it is .839 with 88 per group.

  • As \(|\delta|\) grows, the probability at the plan without assurance falls toward one half, because \(|\hat d|\) exceeds \(|\delta|\) about half the time, and the step adds more cases, as it does when the target narrows: for true_smd = 0.5, a width of 0.30, and assurance = 0.99 the plan moves from 249 to 257 per group, and for true_smd = 1, a width of 0.20, and assurance = 0.90 from 610 to 621.

The noncentral t interval. Kelley and Rausch (2006) plan for the interval from the noncentral t distribution, which ci_smd computes (Kelley, 2007) and ss_aipe_smd plans for; they use the interval with the standard normal quantile only as the starting value of their search (pp. 371–372). The noncentral t interval has exact coverage for the normal model, where the interval of equivalence_smd is a large-sample approximation. At the same \(\hat d\), \(n\), and level the interval of equivalence_smd() is usually the wider of the two: for 90% intervals with \(|\hat d|\) up to 3, by 18 to 30 percent with 3 per group and by less than 1 percent with 100 per group. At the 80 percent level it can be the narrower, by less than 1 percent, when \(|\hat d|\) is 5 or more (equivalence_smd says where the comparison was computed). A study that will report ci_smd() at level \(1 - 2\alpha\) is planned with ss_aipe_smd(conf_level = 1 - 2 * alpha_level).

References

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2006). Sample size planning for the standardized mean difference: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. Psychological Methods, 11(4), 363–385. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.11.4.363

Kelley, K., Maxwell, S. E., & Rausch, J. R. (2003). Obtaining power or obtaining precision: Delineating methods of sample-size planning. Evaluation & the Health Professions, 26(3), 258–287. doi:10.1177/0163278703255242

Lakens, D. (2017). Equivalence tests: A practical primer for t tests, correlations, and meta-analyses. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 8(4), 355–362. doi:10.1177/1948550617697177

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on individual comparisons and Chapter 3 on one-way ANOVA.)

Schuirmann, D. J. (1987). A comparison of the two one-sided tests procedure and the power approach for assessing the equivalence of average bioavailability. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 15(6), 657–680.

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# 1. Plan for a 90% interval on the standardized mean difference of
#    width 0.20, with a planning value of 0.
ss_aipe_equivalence_smd(true_smd = 0, width = 0.20)
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 543  
#>  total_N               1086 
#>  width                 0.200
#>  true_smd              0    
#>  expected_width        0.200
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

# 2. The analysis at the planned size, when the sample standardized mean
#    difference equals the planning value, reports an interval no wider
#    than the target (expected_width is its width).
plan <- ss_aipe_equivalence_smd(true_smd = 0.05, width = 0.20)
n <- plan$value[plan$term == "necessary_n_per_group"]
fit <- equivalence_smd(smd = 0.05, n_1 = n, n_2 = n, smd_upper = 0.3)
fit$value[fit$term == "ci_upper"] - fit$value[fit$term == "ci_lower"]
#> [1] 0.1998534

# 3. With 80% assurance that the realized interval is no wider than 0.20.
#    The last row is the probability at the returned size.
ss_aipe_equivalence_smd(true_smd = 0.05, width = 0.20, assurance = 0.80)
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 543  
#>  total_N               1086 
#>  width                 0.200
#>  true_smd              0.050
#>  expected_width        0.200
#>  assurance             0.800
#>  assurance_attained    0.870
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
